r: The applied competence is interpersonal: leadership, interactive communication, and collaboration practiced through team exercises, plus an orienting survey of advanced-manufacturing career pathways. These map to O*NET activities like communicating with peers, establishing and maintaining interpersonal relationships, and developing and building teams. Task-exposure research classifies interpersonal, team-based work among the low-exposure categories, and observed-usage data shows AI concentrated in computer, mathematical, and writing tasks rather than real-time group collaboration. AI can draft an email or a meeting agenda, but the graded work here is students actually rehearsing collaboration and communication in the room together, which no model performs on their behalf. There is no accreditation or licensure lock specific to this soft-skills survey; embodiment and the interpersonal core do the protective work. At 24 months the instrumental need to develop teamwork and communication competence is intact.

By 2031, AI tools will draft communications, summarize meetings, and coach presentation content, automating preparation around the edges of teamwork. But developing the capacity to lead, negotiate, and collaborate face-to-face is embodied and real-time, sitting in the interpersonal categories task-exposure research places outside AI's reach. Productivity studies show the largest uplift for lower-skilled workers on writing and support tasks, not on the relational judgment this course cultivates. The course's career-orientation content is more exposed, since a model can summarize advanced-manufacturing employment pathways, yet that is a small share of the applied competence. Absent any institutional mandate, embodiment alone holds the instrumental case at Low across this horizon. The rating stays Low; AI shifts document preparation off the student while leaving the human collaboration competence, practiced in teams, untouched.

Over a decade, AI will handle most of the written and informational scaffolding around teamwork, including agendas, summaries, and correspondence, and the survey's career-orientation content will be trivially AI-deliverable, so base automatability ticks up. But the enduring core of the course is embodied interpersonal skill: leading, communicating, and collaborating with other people in real time, which remains among the least automatable activities in the central case through 2036. The honest uncertainty is how much of the surrounding preparation automates, not whether students still need to practice working in teams. Diffusion evidence suggests adoption remains uneven even as capability advances, and relational competence is precisely what manufacturing employers screen for at entry. The rating holds Low; embodiment and the interpersonal task profile keep the instrumental necessity of learning to collaborate intact.
AMS 1010.d: The student will learn the "soft skills" required by industry, such as leadership, interactive communication, and collaboration/teamwork skills, utilizing team exercises and team activities. The course also provides an introduction to Advanced Manufacturing and an overview of the Advanced Manufacturing Sciences (AMS) degree concentration's fit and associated employment potential with Advanced Manufacturing Industries.

r: The applied work splits between CAD modeling and hands-on fabrication: designing 3D objects in software, then operating 3D printers and judging each technology's precision, resolution, and material limits. These map to O*NET activities including drafting and specifying technical parts, designing products, controlling machines and processes, and working with computers. The CAD side is genuinely exposed, as generative-design and AI CAD assistants are improving, but the project-based, hands-on core is embodied: setting up printers, managing failed builds, and developing physical intuition for materials, which task-exposure research places outside AI's automatable range. The course prepares students for an industry Stratasys certification, a voluntary market credential rather than a licensure lock. At 24 months the instrumental need to acquire embodied additive-manufacturing skill is not eroded; AI assists the design step, not the fabrication competence the certification attests.

By 2031, AI generative-design and CAD-automation tools will handle more of the modeling stage, and simulation may offload some pre-print analysis, meaningfully augmenting the design workflow. But the certification this course targets attests hands-on skill: operating printers, diagnosing build failures, and selecting processes for precision and material constraints, an embodied competence that observed-usage data, concentrated in digital knowledge work, does not touch. The jagged-frontier evidence is directly relevant here: an AI-generated model that ignores a printer's real resolution or material behavior fails on the bench, and catching that requires the trained human. No accreditation mandate binds, but embodiment holds the instrumental case. The rating stays Low; the design tasks migrate toward AI while the fabrication and process-judgment competence, which employers and the credential value, remains necessary.

A decade out, AI will be woven through additive-manufacturing design, handling generative geometry, automated print preparation, and parameter optimization, so much routine modeling will be automated and base automatability rises as the digital half of the course erodes. But the embodied half endures: physically operating equipment, troubleshooting real builds, and developing calibrated material intuition are not tasks AI performs on the learner's behalf, and manual/physical work remains low-exposure in the central case through 2036. Industrial additive manufacturing will roboticize further, yet the pedagogical function, a student personally acquiring hands-on competence a certification verifies, is not eliminated. The uncertainty is how much of the design stage automates around a still-embodied fabrication core, not whether students still need bench skill. The rating holds Low, anchored by embodiment and the hands-on, project-based structure.
AMS 3010.d: Students receive industry-endorsed proof of workforce ready Additive Manufacturing skills and knowledge through a program of study in preparation for the certification exam: Proof of skills through assessment. The hands-on, project-based learning (PBL) course will let students design and fabricate 3D objects using computer-aided design (CAD) software and 3D printers. Students will experience the design process and become familiar with the advantages and limitations of each 3D printing technology in terms of precision, resolution, and material capabilities.

r: The internship places students in a real manufacturing workplace under an industry professional for a minimum of forty-five clock hours per credit, with weekly reports, a self-evaluation, and a reflective paper. The applied task is the experiential act of working in the setting itself: performing physical and technical activities, handling equipment and materials, and interacting with a real team. These map to O*NET activities like performing general physical activities, handling and moving objects, and communicating with coworkers, precisely the embodied categories task-exposure research classifies as least exposed. The binding constraint is structural: the clock-hour placement requirement cannot be satisfied by an AI system, and it is a required AMS core component. AI might draft a reflective paragraph, but it cannot accrue the supervised workplace experience the credit represents. At 24 months the instrumental need is fully intact.

By 2031, AI tools will pervade the workplaces students intern in, and the written deliverables, weekly reports and reflective papers, become more automatable, echoing task-exposure research that ranks writing among the most exposed activities. But the core of the internship is embodiment and presence: being physically in a manufacturing environment, doing supervised work, and being evaluated by a human professional. That is not delegable, and the clock-hour requirement is a hard structural lock no capability advance reaches. Observed-usage and diffusion data suggest AI augments the tasks interns perform rather than removing the need to perform them. The rating stays Low; the paperwork around the placement automates while the experiential, in-person requirement, the entire point of the credit, remains necessary and unmet by any model.

Over a decade, workplaces will be more automated and interns will increasingly work alongside AI systems, and the reflective writing deliverables will be largely AI-assisted. Even so, the instrumental function of the internship, accruing supervised, embodied experience in a real manufacturing setting under a human professional, is not a task AI executes for the student, and manual/physical and in-person work remains the least-exposed category in the central case through 2036. The clock-hour structural requirement shows no path to being met by automation. The genuine uncertainty concerns what work interns do once inside, not whether the placement itself is still required. The rating holds Low with high confidence; embodiment and the clock-hour mandate together foreclose erosion of the instrumental need.
AMS 3980.d: Students will have an opportunity to gain work experience under the guidance of an industry professional. Students must complete a minimum of 45 clock hours per credit hour during the semester in a placement relevant to their selected AMS concentration. All internship students will also be required to prepare weekly internship reports, complete a self-evaluation survey and a reflective paper at the completion of the placement. Internship requirements vary by department. For information and instructions on finding and enrolling in an internship, contact the Classroom to Career (C2) Hub at [contact omitted].

By 2031, AI project tools will draft plans, track tasks, and generate deliverable content, automating portions of the individual work inside a team project. But the competence the course builds, collaborating, negotiating roles, and delivering jointly with industry partners in real time, is embodied and interpersonal, sitting outside AI's automatable frontier per task-exposure research. Absent any institutional mandate, embodiment holds the instrumental case across the horizon. The rating stays Low; AI accelerates the artifacts a team produces while leaving the human teamwork and stakeholder-collaboration competence, which is the actual object of the course, necessary. A decade out, AI will handle much of the individual production inside collaborative projects, including drafting, analysis, and scheduling, and base automatability rises as those sub-tasks automate. AMS 4700.d: Students will have an opportunity to gain team project work experience during collaborative projects with industry professionals.

r: The capstone requires students to plan and design an advanced-manufacturing process, producing top-level diagrams, process maps, schedules, outlines, and written instructions spanning process setup, material and equipment acquisition, production planning, quality assurance, and packaging. The deliverables are planning and documentation artifacts, among the more AI-exposed outputs, since task-exposure research ranks writing and structured documentation highly and observed-usage data shows drafting and planning tasks are prominent. Yet the graded competence is integrative manufacturing judgment: understanding how these disciplines fit together into an efficient, safe process. Verification burden is real, since a plausible-looking process plan that fails in production or overlooks a safety constraint is costly and its failure non-obvious. As a senior culminating design experience within an ABET-relevant engineering-technology program, the course is structurally embedded. At 24 months the instrumental need holds; the dampener and accreditation context keep realized erosion at Low.

By 2031, AI will draft process maps, schedules, and written work instructions with facility and propose candidate process designs, eroding the execution rationale for much of the capstone's documentation. GDPval-style evidence shows models approaching but still below expert parity on real occupational deliverables. The jagged frontier is acute here: an AI-generated manufacturing plan can be confidently wrong, overlooking a safety constraint or a production bottleneck, in ways only a competent human detects, so verification keeps the knowledgeable student necessary. The integrative judgment of fitting setup, quality assurance, and packaging into a coherent process is not the automatable part. The ABET-relevant culminating-design requirement holds the course structurally in place across a catalog cycle. The instrumental case shifts from producing the plan to verifying it, and that verification burden together with accreditation context keeps the rating at Low.

A decade out, AI will be embedded across manufacturing planning, generating process documentation, schedules, and preliminary designs, and the central case has it competently performing most of the documentation execution this capstone teaches. The base automatability of the planning deliverables is high, and by 2036 the pure documentation rationale is substantially eroded. What remains is the integrative, safety-aware judgment to specify a sound manufacturing process and to verify that an AI-generated plan will actually run efficiently and safely, a competence that grows more valuable as models produce plausible but uneven candidates. The ABET-relevant culminating-design structure persists absent accreditor change, and verification burden endures. The rating rises to Medium, capped there by that verification role and accreditation context from reaching High. The uncertainty concerns how capstones are taught under pervasive planning AI, not whether integrative manufacturing judgment remains needed.
AMS 4940.d: Students in this course will plan and design an advanced manufacturing process comprised of top-level diagrams, process maps, schedules, outlines, and written instructions. Projects may be developed by the student or assigned by departmental faculty/staff. The project will reflect and identify the disciplines within the field of advanced manufacturing including process setup, planning, material and equipment acquisition, production planning, quality assurance, and packaging - and understand how they work together to achieve a final goal. The final project will demonstrate the general understanding of concepts associated with advanced manufacturing processes to ensure efficient operations, intelligent production, and improve the overall effectiveness of the organization.
